items.title: perf(rides): load only the target track for analysis + geometry-only overlays
items.body:
Batch item #1 of the improvement analysis — the biggest tangible performance win.
## Problem
Opening one ride's analysis collected `getRidesWithTracksFlow()`, which **reassembled and Moshi-parsed the full GPS track of *every* ride** (per-ride length query + chunked `substr` reads + JSON parse), then picked the one by id. The other tracks were never used — `evaluateAchievements` reads only aggregate columns. Worse, the flow keyed off `getAllMetaFlow()`, so it re-ran the whole O(all tracks) work on **any** DB change (rename, bike reassign, archive). The heatmap / ridden-tracks overlays had the same root cause and held every full `RecordedRide` in memory.
## Fix (performance-only — identical results)
- `RideAnalysisViewModel` now `combine`s `getRide(rideId)` (single track, off-thread) with the track-free `getRideSummariesFlow()`; the heavy work (`analyzeRide`, `buildRideMapData`, best efforts, climbs, replay prep) is keyed on a lightweight `TrackKey` so a rename / weather-toggle / bike-reassign only re-projects cheap fields.
- `evaluateAchievements(...)` now takes `List<RecordedRideSummary>` (kept pure).
- New geometry-only `RideTrackGeometry` source (`getRideTrackGeometriesFlow()`, lat/lon only, backed by a new track-free `getTrackKeysFlow()` and gated with `distinctUntilChanged` on the track set) feeds `RideHeatmap`/`RideTrackLines` instead of full ride objects.
## Notes
No user-facing behaviour change. **No schema change** — only a new track-free `@Query` was added. Tests updated + added (achievements Summary signature; VM proves only the target track loads and the PR still comes from summaries; repo geometry mapping). Verified: `:app:testDebugUnitTest`, `:app:lintDebug`, `:app:compileDebugKotlin` all green.

items.body:
Part of #747. **Stacked on #770** (which is stacked on #768) — it builds on the `corner_rank` field that #770 adds to this driver. Review after those merge.

## What is retracted

The #638 showcase table published a six-decimal `E/site` and `dE_ref` per cell. Those columns are removed. Two **independent** defects, either of which alone disqualifies them as physics:

1. **Collapsed environment.** The sweep ran `gs_recipe="1x1"`, whose corner-pair projector collapses the CTM environment to rank-1 corners (#723, #726, #746) — a χ_eff = 1 mean-field boundary that carries no boundary entanglement and does not respond to χ.
2. **Never converged.** All **29** recorded cells are `gs_num_steps=6`, `converged=false`, `is_anchor=false`. The "accurate-AD anchor" cells were never recorded at all. Six optimizer steps cannot support a physics claim under *any* recipe.

Because both are present, the recorded data **cannot** attribute the observed χ-non-monotonicity to the collapse — the two causes are inseparable here. `-0.174648` at D=4, χ=32, 4-GPU is not a physical Heisenberg energy by any reading.

Per the maintainer's call: **retire rather than re-run.** A 6-step sweep would need redoing from scratch regardless of recipe, so regenerating it is not a fix.

## What stays

**All performance results.** `ms/step` and `peak_gb` depend on tensor *shapes*, which the collapse does not change. The D⁶ cost jump, the host→FLOP transition and the multi-GPU crossover all stand, and the two plots (`ms_per_step_vs_chi.png`, `peak_gb_vs_chi.png`) are untouched. No energy plot ever existed — it needs anchor rows, of which there are none.

`scaling_results.csv` keeps the raw values as a historical record; the banner says explicitly not to reinstate the columns from it.

## Preventing a repeat

`results_to_markdown` now renders the energy as `-` for any cell that either did not converge **or** whose `corner_rank` is 1. Combined with the per-cell `corner_rank` that #770 records, an unconverged mean-field energy can no longer reach the published table.

items.title: docs(scale): correct F1 — table-facts RPC slowness is a generic plan + verified one-line fix
items.body:
Corrects the F1 finding in `docs/scale-readiness-review.md` after re-profiling live (read-only). **My original F1 diagnosis was wrong**, and the fix it recommended (rewrite the fuzzy disjunct to the `%` operator) is **already on live and did not help.**

## What's actually happening
- Live `match_document_table_facts_text` already uses the bounded-CTE + `%` form. Each arm is fast in isolation (tsv `@@` 0.36 ms, `normalized_terms &&` 5.5 ms, trigram `%` 158 ms), and the **full body with a literal query runs in 70 ms**.
- But the **RPC call is 5.3 s**. Root cause: the function is `LANGUAGE sql STABLE` **with `SET search_path`** → non-inlinable → its body is planned once with an unknown `$1`, so the planner can't estimate trigram/tsv selectivity and picks near-seq-scan strategies. Every call pays that generic plan.
- Verified on live: `SET plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan` drops it **5.3 s → ~1.1 s (≈4.8×)**.

## The fix (pure performance — results byte-identical, no eval gate)
```sql
alter function public.match_document_table_facts_text(text, integer, uuid[], uuid)
  set plan_cache_mode = 'force_custom_plan';
```
Body-agnostic (targets the function by argument signature), so it does **not** collide with the separate schema.sql↔live body/return-signature drift on this RPC (that reconciliation belongs to the drift backlog). Same one-liner applies to the other non-inlined hybrid RPCs (memory-cards, index-units, embedding-fields). A full ≈75× fix (→ ~70 ms) needs converting to `plpgsql` + `RETURN QUERY EXECUTE`, after the drifted body is reconciled.

## Why docs, not a migration
Applying to live needs the linked `supabase` CLI (operator credentials — not authenticated in this environment) and the migration policy forbids `db push` on this project's divergent history. The `ALTER FUNCTION` above is a safe, results-identical, one-line change you can run in the dashboard SQL editor or land as a committed migration when you next apply migrations.

Refs #339

items.title: ci: fix performance test results parsing
fix(testcontainers): stop a cancelled performance run from leaking its compose stack
items.body: # Why A cancelled performance run leaves its Docker Compose stack running on the CI runner. [This run](https://github.com/opsmill/infrahub-private-tests/actions/runs/31086406302/job/92566782607) is the case that prompted the fix: the cancel signal arrived, `send_results()` was still serializing the report when the follow-up signal landed, pytest died mid-upload, and `infrahub-test-b52f4d8e` was never torn down. The mechanism is a hook-ordering problem. On an interrupted session pytest does **not** tear fixtures down from the test loop — class and session fixtures are finalized by `_pytest.runner`'s `pytest_sessionfinish`. Pluggy runs entry-point plugins *before* core ones, so result reporting was sitting in front of the fixture that stops the stack, and a GitHub runner gives a cancelled step only about 7.5s between signals. Goal: a cancel can no longer cost the stack its shutdown. Non-goals: the workflow-side `if: always()` sweep of leftover `infrahub-test-*` projects, which belongs in `infrahub-private-tests`. That is the only cleanup that survives SIGKILL and is still worth adding — these commits shrink the window, they do not remove the need for a backstop. ## What changed Three commits, each independently reviewable. **`fix: report performance results after the stack teardown`** — marks `pytest_sessionfinish` `trylast` so reporting runs behind the teardown. **`fix: keep result reporting from aborting the session`** — `finalize()` guarded only the HTTP call, and only against `Exception`; the serialization ahead of it was unguarded, so a `KeyboardInterrupt` there escaped `wrap_session`'s `finally` and took the process down before pytest finished unwinding. Now the whole reporting path is guarded against `BaseException`, and an interrupted session is not reported at all — those numbers cover part of the suite, and the remaining seconds belong to the teardown. **`perf: encode the performance payload once per upload`** — the payload embeds every metric series scraped over the run, so it grows with run length and dominates the session-finish path. It was encoded twice (once for the checksum, again by httpx for the body). Now encoded once, with the envelope assembled around those bytes, plus an explicit upload timeout instead of httpx's 5s default. What stayed the same: the checksum contract. It still covers a compact encoding of the payload value, so a receiver that re-encodes the parsed payload verifies exactly as before — the difference is that those bytes are now also the bytes on the wire. Envelope key order changes (`data` moves last); no other API change. ## How to review Start with `plugin.py` — the `trylast` marker and the `INTERRUPTED` early return are the whole behavioral fix. `_serialize_request()` in `performance_test.py` is the part worth extra scrutiny: it splices pre-encoded bytes into the envelope rather than handing httpx a dict, and `test_request_checksum_covers_the_payload_on_the_wire` reproduces the receiver's verification to pin that down. `test_reporting_runs_after_the_stack_teardown` asserts the hook order directly, so a future plugin change that reintroduces the bug fails a test rather than a production run. ## How to test ```bash cd python_testcontainers && uv sync --all-groups uv run pytest --rootdir=. -c pyproject.toml -q tests ``` The cancellation itself was reproduced out of tree by driving a real pytest session with a class-scoped fixture and a slow `send_results`, sending SIGINT and then a second SIGINT 3s later: | | exit | teardown ran? | |---|---|---| | before | `-2` (killed mid-upload) | **no** — stack leaks | | after | `2` (clean `INTERRUPTED`) | **yes** | ## Impact & rollout - **Backward compatibility:** checksum verification unchanged; envelope key order changes. No change to any collected metric. - **Performance:** halves payload encoding on the session-finish path. - **Config/env changes:** none. - **Deployment notes:** safe to deploy; `infrahub-testcontainers` only, no server-side code touched. ## Checklist - [x] Tests added/updated - [ ] Changelog entry — not applicable, `python_testcontainers`-only changes carry no fragment by existing convention - [ ] External docs updated — n/a - [ ] Internal .md docs updated — n/a - [x] I have reviewed AI generated content

- `gcl/materialize.*` — reworked into incremental hopper memoization (the direction our Addendum 2 argued for).
- `gcl/optimizer.*` — rewritten query optimization, now **default-on** (`gcl/gcl.cc:47`), so our jsonl query/server inherit it automatically at hopper-construction time.

Charlie's new hopper/optimizer tests, swept into `//test:tests` via the glob) and the isj suite (140 passed / 1 skipped) green.

| query | before | after | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| A/B killer tier (1M) | 2.25s | 0.28s | 8× |
| tier2 — three deadly phrases (100M) | ~712s | 152s | 4.7× |

items.title: Surface empty BCPT results as a warning instead of silent success
items.body:
## Problem

When BCPT performance tests run but produce no log entries (for example, because the test runner exits early, the suite codeunit IDs do not match the published app, or the job fails silently), the results file contains no entries. \GetBcptSummaryMD\ returned an empty string, the \AnalyzeTests\ step wrote nothing to the job summary, and the build succeeded with no indication that performance tests did not produce output.

Fixes #2158

## Changes

### Actions/AnalyzeTests/TestResultAnalyzer.ps1

- \GetBcptSummaryMD\: Distinguish between the results file not existing (return empty string, no test was run) and the results file existing but containing no entries (return an informational message). The message is written to the GitHub step summary under the Performance test results heading, making the empty result visible.

### Actions/AnalyzeTests/AnalyzeTests.ps1

- After calling \GetBcptSummaryMD\, check whether the results file is present but the summary is still empty. Emit a \::Warning::\ annotation in that case as a defence-in-depth measure.

### Tests/AnalyzeTests.Test.ps1

- Add tests for \ReadBcptFile\ when the file does not exist and when it exists but contains no entries.
- Add a test for \GetBcptSummaryMD\ verifying that it returns an empty string when the file does not exist and a non-empty warning message when the file exists but contains no entries.

## Testing

1. Create a BCPT test app and configure a suite with codeunit IDs that do not match any published app.
2. Run the AL-Go pipeline so that \RunBCPTTests.ps1\ exits without recording measurements.
3. Before this fix: the Performance test results step writes nothing to the summary and the build succeeds silently.
4. After this fix: the summary shows a message stating that no BCPT results were recorded, and a warning annotation appears on the step.

You can also run the Pester test suite locally:

items.title: fix(lens): the console carries its own scrim — legibility must not depend on the scene
items.body:
## The bug (CEO drill, 4 Aug evening)

The fps readout and the sync-trim buttons were rendering but **unreadable** over her white-and-yellow wall — she reported them as "not rendering clearly" and could not use the trim at all. Screenshots in the drill log.

## Root cause

The fidelity readout and trim controls wear dark slate text (`#4A5568`, `#64748B`) and near-black borders (`#1A1A2E`) — colors designed for the dark idle page — floated at 60% cinematic opacity over live video, protected only by a **dark text-shadow**. A dark shadow behind dark text over a bright scene protects nothing: the shadow was a bet that the scene is dark, and the product's background is whatever the camera sees. The proof is in the same frame: the mode toggle and live strip, which carry their own dark pill backgrounds, stayed readable.

## Fix, generalized

- One `lens-console` wrapper around every control and readout. In cinematic mode it carries a contained scrim — `rgba(7,9,20,.6)` + 18px backdrop-blur + hairline border — so legibility is independent of the scene. Outside cinematic mode the class is inert.
- The washed rows get honest dark-ground colors: readout/trim `#94A3B8`, trim value `#E2E8F0`, button borders `#475569` (+hover), budget `#7C8AA5`.
- Same-day drill log rides along (doctrine rule 2): her screenshots answered both open §6 questions — **19fps delivered** (Chrome and Edge agree, matching the headless probe's 18) and trim untouched at 700ms *because* the control was unreadable.

items.title: Fix /tbr and /books page load performance
items.body:
Fixes two independent, empirically-measured performance problems reported by the user ("why does navigating to the manage all books and tbr gap pages take so long?").

Root-caused by direct measurement before any fix was written — see `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-25-performance-fixes-design.md`.

## Results

Measured at realistic scale (900 owned books × 808 TBR items, matching the real Goodreads TBR count):

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `getTbrGap()` per request | **49,267ms** | **13ms** |
| `/tbr` page load | **51.2s** cold | **~70ms** |
| `/books` page load | 2.3–2.9s, 4.3MB HTML | **~110ms, 139KB** |
| Full fuzzy cross-product | every request | **once, on demand** |

## `/tbr` — persist ownership instead of recomputing it

`computeTbrGap()` fuzzy-matched every TBR item against every owned book **on every request**. `GoodreadsTbrItem` now has an `owned` column, maintained incrementally:

- Two new maintainers in `tbrGap.ts`: `markTbrItemsOwnedByTitle(title)` (new owned title appears) and `recheckOwnedTbrItems()` (owned title disappears).
- Called from **all 7 paths** that create/delete/retitle a `Book`: `books.ts` (scan/add + edit), `absSync.ts` (create + delete-on-zero-copies), `ownedPhysicalSync.ts`, `duplicates.ts` (merge), `copies.ts` (last-copy delete). Every call runs *after* its write commits — `recheckOwnedTbrItems` reads the live `Book` table, so running it first would no-op.
- `reconcileTbrItems` computes `owned` for shelf items it creates, and recomputes only when a title actually changed.
- `computeTbrGap` is now a single `WHERE owned = false` query.

**The `unstable_cache` / `revalidateTag` layer is removed entirely.** With the query cheap, it was pure complexity — and it had a latent bug: cron-triggered syncs could never call `revalidateTag` (no request context), so they silently relied on the 30-minute TTL. Now there's no staleness window for any sync path.

Note the established "cheap-exact-tier + capped-fuzzy-fallback" pattern used in `reconcileTbrItems`/`findDuplicateBookGroups` was considered and rejected here: a TBR item almost never *exactly* matches an owned title (that's the whole point of the fuzzy check), so a cap would silently misclassify owned books as unread.

## `/books` — pagination

The query was already fast (74ms); the cost was rendering the entire catalog. Added an opt-in `limit` to `searchCatalog` (unused by the home-page caller, so its behavior is unchanged) and a "Load more" link on `/books`, 50 per page, preserving all active filters.

## Recompute ownership button

`/tbr` gets a **"Recompute ownership"** button (`POST /api/tbr/recompute-ownership`). This covers the initial post-migration backfill and repairs any future drift. It corrects `owned` in **both** directions, only writes rows that actually change, and is safely idempotent. `scripts/backfill-tbr-owned.ts` calls the same function, so there's one implementation rather than two that can diverge.

## Deployment note

The migration defaults `owned` to `false`, so every pre-existing TBR item reads as unowned until a full recompute runs once. **After deploying, click "Recompute ownership" on `/tbr`** (or run `npm run backfill:tbr-owned`). The incremental hooks handle everything that changes afterward.

## Test plan

- [x] 343 tests passing (up from 316), `npm run build` clean, `npm run lint` unchanged (2 pre-existing findings in untouched files)
- [x] Perf measured directly at 900×808 scale in the isolated test DB
- [x] `/books` verified in a browser across 7 cases: page boundaries (50 → 100 → all 120, link correctly absent at the end), invalid `limit` fallback (`0`, `abc`), and filter round-tripping (`q`, `types`)
- [x] `/tbr` verified in a browser: owned items correctly hidden; the recompute button fixed two deliberately-drifted rows (one wrongly owned, one wrongly unowned) in one click, and reported "everything was already correct" on a second click

## Summary

- Add `bootstorm_time` boot time measurement to `WinstressVm` and `LinstressVm`, using **exactly the same calculation as `BootstormVM`**

| Start timer | `_set_bootstorm_vm_start_time(vm_name)` |
| Wait for SSH access | `_wait_vm_access(vm_name)` |

items.title: perf: strip model_snapshot from non-full saves; add live save-timer UX
items.body:
Root cause
----------
Every simulation run was serialised with the full model embedded as
_model_snapshot inside results_json, regardless of detail level.
For Glasgow Central the model_json alone is ~290 KB, making a typical
INSERT payload ~300 KB — 98% of which was redundant data the DB already
holds in des_models.model_json.  That large JSONB write pushed Supabase
save times above 30 s and triggered unhealthy-warming alerts.

Fixes — Task 1 (performance)
-----------------------------
* results-persistence.js: resolve detailLevel BEFORE the runRecord block
  so _model_snapshot is only embedded when detailLevel === "full".
  All default ("minimal") and "compact" saves now skip the snapshot.
* execute/index.jsx (all three save paths): pass
  { includeModelSnapshot: effectiveResultDetailLevel === "full" }
  to buildRunRecord so the expensive JSON.parse/stringify deep-clone of
  the model is never performed for normal saves either.
Expected payload reduction for Glasgow Central: ~300 KB → ~5-15 KB.

Fixes — Task 2 (UX during slow saves)
--------------------------------------
* Added module-level doCloudSave() helper that:
  - Shows a live elapsed-time counter (updates every 1 s)
  - Escalates message at 5 s: "taking longer than usual"
  - Escalates message at 15 s: "Supabase may be starting up"
  - Wraps the Supabase call in try/catch and surfaces errors in the
    save-status banner and run log (the step-by-step path previously
    had no try/catch at all)
* All three cloud-save paths now use doCloudSave() — identical UX.

## Reduce sustained CPU usage (WindowServer) when running terminals

Cate showed high sustained CPU even while idle — WindowServer (the macOS compositor) was elevated. This PR targets the two independent drivers behind that, plus a correctness bug found along the way.

Together these changes reduced the CPU usage from a constant ~45% to ~2%-3%. 

Monitoring experiments showed between 16x and 24x efficiency improvement. Between 94% and 96% less WindowServer (mac) utilization. 
  
## process-spawn churn (main process)

The shell activity poller spawned a burst of short-lived processes every 1 second, per terminal — including a system-wide lsof socket-table scan.

- Fix a broken lsof invocation (shell.ts, terminal.ts). lsof ORs its selection filters by default, so lsof -p <pid> -d cwd did
not mean "the cwd of this pid". It scanned every process on the system, and the parser returned the first match (a low-pid daemon at /). Added -a to AND the filters: this fixes a user-facing bug and turns an ~800-process scan into a 1-process
lookup.
- Scope the listening-port scan to terminal PIDs. scanListeningPorts enumerated the entire system's TCP socket table every cycle, then discarded everything that wasn't a terminal PID. It now passes the already-computed PID list via -a -p <pids>,
inspecting only the terminals' process trees. (Parsing now tolerates lsof exit 1, which it returns when some pids have no
listening sockets.)
- Split the poll cadence. The lightweight agent-detection scan stays at 1s (it drives activity indicators and the "needs
input" / "finished" notifications). The heavier lsof work (cwd + ports) moved to a separate 5s timer.
- Focus-gate the cwd scan. The cwd scan only backs an on-demand "Copy Working Directory" action, so it's skipped entirely while no app window is focused. (The port scan still runs every 5s regardless — it's cheap now and surfaces dev-server ports that come up in the background.)

## WindowServer / compositor cost (renderer)

WindowServer was pegged with calm paint flashing, the signature of GPU layers being composited every frame rather than repainted. The cause: continuous, always-on animations, made expensive by compositing them over a live backdrop-filter.

- Remove the sidebar backdrop-filter: blur. A live backdrop blur forces the compositor to re-sample everything behind the
sidebar on every frame anything underneath changes, and any continuous animation in that layer re-triggers the blur every frame. Replaced with a static, near-opaque translucent fill (88% → 96%) that reads as the same frosted surface without per-frame compositing.
- Flatten perpetual sidebar/tab animations to static indicators:
  - "Awaiting input" indicator → static dot (removed the infinitely-pulsing scale/opacity ring + dot).
  - "Running" label shimmer (cate-notif-pulse) → static color (removed the looping gradient sweep, which also re-painted text every frame). Shared class, so the agent chat thread "Thinking/Loading/running" labels are now static too.
  - Sidebar header "busy" button → static dimming instead of animate-spin.
- Make terminal cursor blink opt-in (default off), with a Settings → Terminal toggle. A blinking cursor keeps the compositor
awake. Added window-focus gating so a focused terminal's blink pauses when the app isn't frontmost (xterm otherwise keeps blinking the last-focused terminal in the background). Toggling the setting applies live to open terminals.

## Other Fixes

- git.test.ts assumed git init creates a master branch and then checkout -b main. On modern git (default init.defaultBranch=main) the branch already exists and the test fatals. Switched to git branch -M main, robust regardless of the default branch name.
- Bug fix — "Copy Working Directory" always returned /. The workspace-tab right-click action (and the cwd tracking behind it) copied / instead of the terminal's real directory, because the lsof cwd lookup was missing -a and parsed an unrelated system process. Adding -a returns the correct directory.

## Notes / follow-ups

  - WindowServer cost scales with display resolution/refresh rate; the win is largest on Retina/ProMotion displays.
  - Static cate-notif-pulse is global, so the agent chat "Thinking/Loading" shimmer is now static too — intentional, easy to
  scope back to the sidebar if the chat shimmer is wanted.
  - Other transient spinners (GitPanel, BrowserPanel, AgentPanel) were left as-is — short-lived, not sustained drivers.
  - Possible follow-up: make "Copy Working Directory" fully lazy (fetch cwd on click) and drop the cwd poll entirely.

items.title: Fix search performance and empty results
items.body:
## Problem
Search in the Find section was non-performant and often showed empty results.

## Root Cause
**SwiftUI reactivity was broken.** `FinderViewModel.sites` and `isSearching` were computed properties reading from `finderService`, but since `finderService` itself wasn't `@Published`, SwiftUI never detected changes. The view simply never re-rendered when results arrived.

## Changes
- **Fix reactivity**: ViewModel now uses Combine `assign(to:)` to pipe `finderService`'s `@Published` properties into its own `@Published` properties, so SwiftUI properly observes changes
- **Concurrent searches**: MKLocalSearch queries now run via `TaskGroup` instead of sequentially (~4x faster for 'All' filter which runs 4 queries)
- **Cache TTL**: Added 5-minute expiry to prevent stale results
- **Search cancellation**: New searches cancel in-flight ones
- **Error UI**: Search failures now show a retry button instead of being silently swallowed

items.title: Stream the Set Status bulk action with Db::each() to avoid OOM
items.body:
Fixes #19070

**Problem**
Currently, `SetStatus::performAction()` loads the entire selection into memory using `$query->all()` and holds it during the `saveElement()` loop. This causes peak memory to grow linearly with the selection size, meaning large bulk status changes easily hit the `memory_limit` (HTTP 500). See #19070 for a repro.

**Solution**
This PR switches the query to stream the elements using `Db::each()`, exactly like `Elements::resaveElements()` does. This ensures each element is freed from memory right after it gets saved. 

This is strictly a performance fix: events, validation, revisions, and results remain completely unchanged. With this fix, the ~9,500-entry selection from the issue completes with a stable ~175 MB peak instead of crashing partway through.

*Note:* Since we no longer have an array to count, I added a `$total` query to replace `count($elements)`. This ensures the 'all failed' check and singular/plural flash messages continue to work exactly as before.

items.title: [Performance] Cache normalizeHeaderName results and fix irregular header acronyms (ETag, Content-MD5)
items.body:
## Summary

Two birds, one stone: performance optimization **#287** + code-quality fix **#354**.

### What changed in `normalizeHeaderName()`

**Before:** Every response header went through `explode()` + `array_map(ucfirst())` + `implode()` — roughly 3–5 string allocations per header, recomputed from scratch on every response.

**After:** A `static` lookup cache stores the normalized form keyed by lowercase input. First request pays the cost; subsequent requests are O(1) — at most 1 normalization per unique header name across the entire worker lifetime. The cache is bounded by the cardinality of header names (a finite, low-cardinality set).

### Irregular header corrections

| Input | Before (ucfirst) | After |
|---|---|---|
| `etag` | `Etag` | **`ETag`** |
| `content-md5` | `Content-Md5` | **`Content-MD5`** |
| `www-authenticate` | `Www-Authenticate` | **`WWW-Authenticate`** |
| `dnt` | `Dnt` | **`DNT`** |

Per RFC 9110, HTTP header names are case-insensitive, so the old forms were valid — the corrections just match common usage.

### Tests added

- `testConvertNormalizesIrregularHeaderNames` — verifies each correction produces the canonical form
- `testConvertNormalizesIrregularHeadersConsistentlyOnRepeatedCalls` — confirms cache returns correct value for different values under the same header name across multiple `convert()` calls
- `testConvertPreservesRegularHeaderCasingAfterCaching` — proves cache population does not affect regular headers
- `testConvertNormalizesMixedRegularAndIrregularHeaders` — ensures regular + irregular headers coexist correctly

No behavioural change for headers that already canonicalise correctly.

Closes #287
Closes #354

## Problem
The weekly competitor intelligence was reaching the Slack digest and the copy/angle LLM prompts, but was **not** wired into a tracked, measured experiment. The `ExperimentScientistAgent` built for exactly this was **dead code** (zero call sites), and the LinkedIn creative-performance readback query was **broken** (`invalid identifier 'C.CREATIVE_URN'`).

## What this does
Closes the loop: competitor intel → prioritized backlog → pinned challenger arm (angle C) → live LinkedIn CTR readback → weekly Slack "Experiment Results" → outcome recorded.

- **Activate the scientist** — competitor `experiment_ideas` become a persistent, prioritized `ExperimentBacklog`; the top insight is pinned to `data/experiment_directive.json` (new `src/competitor_experiment.py`). Fixes an `ingest_feedback` early-return that skipped competitor ideas when there were no feedback hypotheses.
- **Challenger arm** — `directive_prompt_block` pins angle C to the pinned insight in `brief_generator` + `figma_creative` (A/B stay baseline).
- **Readback** — `read_results` compares challenger vs baseline LinkedIn CTR per cohort and records win/loss on the backlog; new step E in the weekly loop posts an "Experiment Results" section. **Fixes `CREATIVE_PERFORMANCE_SQL`** against the real `SCALE_PROD.VIEW.LINKEDIN_CREATIVE_COSTS` schema + a deduped conversions join; `angle`/`photo_subject` enriched from the registry (they don't exist in Snowflake).
- **Per-insight attribution** — append-only `experiment_id` registry column, centrally auto-stamped on angle-C rows in `log_campaign`; readback filters the challenger to the pinned experiment (falls back to an angle-C proxy, clearly labeled).
- **Fix garbage ideas** — sanitize the ramp-summary seed via `_clean_tg_label` + guard the SEO recommendation so leaked requester asks (cohort tables, pay rates, campaign ids) never become "ideas".

## Verified
- Live: readback produced a real verdict — GMR-0019 Clinical Medicine angle C **0.62%** vs A/B **0.55%** → **+12.4%** winner.
- **55 tests passing** (new `test_competitor_experiment.py` + `test_competitor_intel_clean.py`; updated weekly-loop tests).

The angle enrichment reads the **local** `campaign_registry.json`, so CI needs that file present/fresh. TikTok/Reddit stay creative-only (challenger ships + tagged; results read manually).

items.title: Add forward-since-freeze columns to the Filter A/B tracker
items.body:
The A/B table's numbers are cumulative since late June, which makes them a slow-moving and partly in-sample read: every candidate rule (the 10% edge cut, the 10¢ price floor, the 1.5 °C distance threshold…) was chosen by inspecting the same settled sample the table scores it on, so an all-time lead is not promotion evidence.

Each row now carries:

- **Frozen** — the date the row entered the tracker, hard-coded from the commit that added it (`git log -S` per row name: originals 07-05, raw-edge rows 07-13, pilot-shaped 07-19, edge/price/segment-λ 07-26, distance 08-05).
- **Fwd ROI · n** — that config's ROI (PnL / capital risked) and trade count on targets **strictly after** its freeze date, i.e. days whose outcomes were unknowable when the rule was chosen. Sliced from the same full-history replay, so the walk-forward λ each trade used is unchanged.
- **Default, same window** — the default config replayed on the identical window, so the comparison can't be moved by which weeks happen to fall inside a candidate's window.

First forward read on today's captures:

| Config | All-time | Forward (since freeze) | Default, same window |
|---|---|---|---|
| shrunk + edge ≥ 10% | +20.1% | **+26.4% · 39** | +11.0% · 123 |
| shrunk + SELL + edge ≥ 10% | +24.2% | +31.6% · 30 | +11.0% · 123 |
| shrunk + price ≥ 0.10 | +11.3% | +12.6% · 96 | +11.0% · 123 |
| segment λ | +6.5% | **+5.9% · 159** | +11.0% · 123 |
| distance ≥ 1.5 °C | +18.0% | +50.0% · 2 | +14.7% · 9 |

The edge ≥ 10% family genuinely leads out-of-sample (thin n); the price floor's all-time lead mostly evaporates forward; segment λ's prototype lift has not survived contact; distance is too young to read.

Also: `since()` helper with a unit test (strictly-after semantics), explainer paragraph under the table rewritten to describe the two views, CLAUDE.md updated with the first forward read.
